section.title: Zacchaeus and the Parable of the Minas
section.sectionRationale: In Jericho, a despised chief tax collector climbs a tree to see Jesus and is stunned to hear the Lord invite Himself to his house; Zacchaeus repents with joy, and Jesus declares that salvation has come, for the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Then, because the crowd expects the kingdom to appear at once, Jesus tells of a nobleman who goes to receive a kingdom and returns to reckon with servants entrusted with money and with citizens who rejected him. Grace saves the lost, and the King who is going away will surely return to judge.
section.thesis: The Son of Man seeks and saves the lost, transforming even a chief tax collector by grace, and He is the King who goes to receive His kingdom and will return to reward faithfulness, judge fruitless fear, and destroy those who refused His reign.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the salvation of Zacchaeus; and the parable of the ten minas, on faithfulness while the King is away and the reckoning at His return.

units.label: The salvation of Zacchaeus
units.note: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost

verses.text: Then Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through.
And there was a man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, who was very wealthy.
He was trying to see who Jesus was, but could not see over the crowd because he was small in stature.
So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him, since Jesus was about to pass that way.
When Jesus came to that place, He looked up and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today.”
So Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully.
And all who saw this began to grumble, saying, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!”
But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.”
Jesus said to him, “Today {{soteria|salvation}} has come to this house, because this man too is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to {{zeteo|seek}} and to save the {{apollymi|lost}}.”

units.label: The parable of the ten minas
units.note: well done, good servant; and, slay my enemies

verses.text: While the people were listening to this, Jesus proceeded to tell them a parable, because He was near Jerusalem and they thought the kingdom of God would appear imminently.
So He said, “A man of noble birth went to a distant country to lay claim to his kingship and then return.
Beforehand, he called ten of his servants and gave them ten minas. ‘Conduct business with this until I return,’ he said.
But his subjects hated him and sent a delegation after him to say, ‘We do not want this man to rule over us.’
When he returned from procuring his kingship, he summoned the servants to whom he had given the money, to find out what each one had earned.
The first servant came forward and said, ‘Master, your mina has produced ten more minas.’
His master replied, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been {{pistos|faithful}} in a very small matter, you shall have authority over ten cities.’
The second servant came and said, ‘Master, your mina has made five minas.’
And to this one he said, ‘You shall have authority over five cities.’
Then another servant came and said, ‘Master, here is your mina, which I have laid away in a piece of cloth.
For I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man. You withdraw what you did not deposit and reap what you did not sow.’
His master replied, ‘You wicked servant, I will judge you by your own words. So you knew that I am a harsh man, withdrawing what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow?
Why then did you not deposit my money in the bank, and upon my return I could have collected it with interest?’
Then he told those standing by, ‘Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has ten minas.’
‘Master,’ they said, ‘he already has ten!’
He replied, ‘I tell you that everyone who has will be given more; but the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.
And these enemies of mine who were unwilling for me to rule over them, bring them here and slay them in front of me.’”

soteria.gloss: Salvation, rescue, deliverance. Jesus announces that today salvation has come to Zacchaeus's house, not as a reward for the man's repayment but as the gracious arrival of God's rescue in the person of Jesus. The changed life that follows is the evidence, not the cause, of a salvation that has come.

zeteo.gloss: To seek, to look for. The mission statement of the Gospel, the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, casts Jesus as the seeking Savior. Zacchaeus climbs a tree to see Jesus, but it is Jesus who has been seeking him; the initiative and the search belong to God.

apollymi.gloss: To be lost, to perish. The lost are those perishing away from God, and Zacchaeus, rich yet despised and cut off, is exactly such a one. Jesus came for people like him, not for those who imagine they are found, and He restores this lost son of Abraham to the family of faith.

pistos.gloss: Faithful, trustworthy. The servants who put the master's mina to work are praised as faithful in a very small matter and given authority over cities. Faithfulness with what the absent King entrusts, however small it seems, is what He will reward at His return; fearful inaction is judged as wickedness.

basic.context: As Jesus passes through Jericho, Zacchaeus, a wealthy chief tax collector despised as a traitor and cheat, climbs a sycamore tree just to catch sight of Him. Jesus stops, looks up, and invites Himself to stay at the man's house. The crowd grumbles that Jesus is the guest of a sinner, but Zacchaeus, transformed, pledges half his goods to the poor and fourfold repayment to anyone he has cheated. Jesus declares that salvation has come to this house, for the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Then, because the crowd expects the kingdom to arrive instantly as they near Jerusalem, Jesus tells of a nobleman who leaves to receive a kingdom, entrusts money to his servants, and returns to reward the faithful, judge the servant who hid his mina in fear, and destroy the citizens who refused his rule.
basic.hermeneutics: The two scenes belong together. Zacchaeus shows what salvation looks like: grace seeks the lost, and repentance and generosity follow. The parable corrects the crowd's timing: the kingdom will not appear all at once; the King must go away, and there will be a long interval of faithful stewardship before He returns to reckon and to reign.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus announces soteria, salvation, has come to Zacchaeus's house, God's rescue arriving in person. He states His mission: the Son of Man came to zeteo, to seek, and to save the apollymi, the lost, those perishing away from God. And in the parable the servants judged good are those who were pistos, faithful, with the little entrusted to them while the King was away.
basic.typology: Zacchaeus, a son of Abraham restored, pictures the true children of Abraham marked by faith, not merely descent. The nobleman going to a far country to receive a kingdom and returning echoes both the historical Herods and, more deeply, Christ's ascension and second coming. The rejected king points to the Messiah his own people would not have reign over them.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Son of Man who seeks and saves the lost, the friend of sinners whose mere presence brings salvation into a house. And He is the noble King who goes to a distant country to receive His kingship, entrusts His servants with responsibility, and will return to reward, to judge, and to reign, whether His subjects welcome Him or refuse Him.
basic.god: God takes the initiative to save, seeking out the very people the religious despise. He is generous, entrusting real responsibility to His servants, and just, rewarding faithfulness and judging fruitless fear and outright rebellion. His salvation is free, and His reign is certain.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 34 promises that God will seek the lost sheep. Luke 15 tells three parables of the lost being found. Matthew 25 gives the parallel parable of the talents. Acts 1 recounts the King going away, to return as He left.
basic.oneStory: Just before Jerusalem, Jesus embodies His whole mission by saving a lost tax collector, then warns that the kingdom will not dawn instantly; the King must go and return. The story runs from grace that seeks the lost to the certain reckoning of the King, so His people live faithfully in the interval, longing for His reign.

context.literary:
The two halves of this passage are joined by a single hinge, the phrase in verse 11, While the people were listening to this. The parable is spoken in the same breath as the saying about salvation, to the same crowd, in the same house or doorway of Jericho. Luke wants us to read the sinner who is welcomed and the servant who is judged as one lesson on what the kingdom is like before the King returns.

The Zacchaeus story is shaped around verbs of seeing and being seen. He wants to see who Jesus is, verse 3, runs ahead and climbs, verse 4, and it is Jesus who looks up and sees him, verse 5. The crowd sees too, and what it sees is a sinner being honoured, verse 7. The seeking that Zacchaeus began turns out to have been begun first by the Son of Man, verse 10. The story moves from the rich man's effort to a divine necessity, I must stay at your house today, and the word today then returns in verse 9, Today salvation has come, in a pattern Luke has used since Jesus' first sermon at Nazareth, 4:21, and will use again to the thief on the cross, 23:43.

Beside the ruler of chapter 18 the story is a deliberate pair. Both men are rich and both meet Jesus within a few verses of each other on the way into and through Jericho. The ruler asks what to do and goes away sad, 18:23. Zacchaeus asks nothing, is called by name, and receives Jesus gladly, 19:6. One walks away from the kingdom with his wealth, the other enters it by letting go of half, and the reader is meant to feel the gap.

The parable of the minas is built as a double story, the nobleman and his servants running alongside the nobleman and his enemies. The strands separate in the final scene: the servants are reckoned with in verses 15 to 26 and the enemies are dealt with in verse 27. The three servants who give accounts, with ten, five and one, are a narrower version of the ten in verse 13. The last servant speaks a fatal speech, and the master judges him by his own words, verse 22. The whole unit closes the journey narrative that began at 9:51, and the next verse, 19:28, turns at once to the last stage of the road.
context.historical:
Jericho was the gateway to Jerusalem for the pilgrim traffic from Galilee and the lands east of the Jordan, and the Herods kept a winter palace complex there. A customs post in such a town was a lucrative one. Rome let out the right to collect dues to the highest bidder, and a chief tax collector, the Greek word is architelones, ran a team of subordinates and kept what he gathered above the contract. Luke says Zacchaeus was very wealthy, verse 2, and everyone in the crowd would have drawn the conclusion that he had become rich through taking more than he should. His fellow Jews would have regarded him as ritually and morally unclean, which is why their grumbling in verse 7 is directed at Jesus for becoming the guest of a sinful man.

The law's rules about repaying theft explain the weight of Zacchaeus's offer. The Torah asked for the principal plus a fifth when a man confessed a wrong, Leviticus 6:5, and Numbers 5:7, and in cases of stolen livestock demanded four or five times the value, Exodus 22:1. David's own judgement in 2 Samuel 12:6 was that a man who stole a lamb should pay four times over. So Zacchaeus does not offer to repay what justice demanded of a confessed offender; he offers the higher figure that the law reserved for stolen sheep and oxen, and he adds a gift of half his goods to the poor on top of it.

The parable draws on a story that the audience in Jericho knew well. When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his rule confirmed by Augustus, and a delegation of Jews went after him to ask that he not be made king. Jericho was a place associated with the Herodian family, so a story of a nobleman who goes to a far country for a kingship and is followed by a hostile deputation would have sounded close to home. Jesus does not endorse the nobleman's cruelty. He borrows the setting to say that the King is going away and will come back.

A mina was a large sum, a hundred denarii, which was about three months' pay for a labourer. Ten servants given one each were being trusted with something substantial but not enormous, and the reward of cities in verse 17 is out of all proportion to the amount, a sign of the kingdom's generosity. Banking, the trapeza in verse 23, was a familiar way to earn interest without risk.
context.canonical:
The seeking of the lost is as old as the first question God asked in the garden, Where are you?, Genesis 3:9. Ezekiel 34 gives it its fullest Old Testament form: God Himself says He will search for His sheep and seek them out, verse 11, and will bring back the strayed and bind up the injured, verse 16. Luke 15 had already given three parables of seeking, the sheep, the coin and the son. Verse 10 states in one sentence what those stories dramatise, and the Son of Man here takes the divine shepherd's own role.

Zacchaeus is called a son of Abraham, verse 9, and that belongs to a larger line in Luke. John the Baptist told the crowds that God could raise up children for Abraham from stones, 3:8, and Jesus healed a woman and called her a daughter of Abraham, 13:16. Paul later argues that those who have faith are sons of Abraham, Galatians 3:7, and that Abraham himself was counted righteous when he believed, Romans 4:3. A despised tax collector in Jericho is thereby shown to belong to the family God had promised to bless.

The parable of the minas has a close relative in Matthew's parable of the talents, Matthew 25:14 to 30. The two stories share a master going away, servants entrusted with money, a reckoning, a servant who buries his sum and a rule that those who have will be given more. They also differ in several details. Luke has ten servants each given the same, a rival delegation and a king's vengeance on his enemies. Luke's unique elements make the story about the kingdom's delay and reception, which is why he says in verse 11 that it was told to correct a mistaken expectation.

Reckoning at the master's return runs through the rest of the New Testament. Paul writes that each will give an account to God, Romans 14:12, and that the works of believers will be tested, 1 Corinthians 3:12 to 15. Peter calls on believers to serve one another as good stewards of God's varied grace, 1 Peter 4:10. The enemies who refuse the King in verse 27 find their echo in Psalm 2, where the nations who rebel against the LORD's anointed are warned, and in Revelation 19, where the King of kings comes to judge.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see that Jesus will eat with anyone, and that when He does, salvation arrives. The crowd murmurs because Jesus is the guest of a sinner, and Luke has just recorded the same murmuring at the start of chapter 15. His answer in verse 10 is a statement of Jesus' purpose, and the story of Zacchaeus is a living example. The kingdom is for the lost, and the lost are not only the poor and the sick but a rich collaborator whom no one would have chosen.

The second purpose is to correct a mistaken timetable. Verse 11 tells us plainly that Jesus told the parable because they thought the kingdom was about to appear at once. Luke is writing for a church that had waited a long time after the resurrection for the King's return, and the parable tells them they should not be surprised. The King has gone, and the interval is for work. The servants are given a trust, and what they do with it will be examined.

Luke also wants to show how the two halves meet. Zacchaeus is a servant who uses his wealth faithfully after receiving the King, whereas the third servant buries his out of fear. A man who is welcomed by grace gives freely. A man who thinks the master is harsh hoards. Luke's readers are meant to ask which of the two pictures describes them, and whether they know the master as Zacchaeus knew Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The story of Zacchaeus is a description and not a template. Jesus did not ask him to give half his goods, and the man volunteered it. Nor does the passage turn the offer into a rule for tax collectors or for rich people, though it does show what a changed heart tends to do with money. The same Jesus told another rich man to sell everything, 18:22, so there is no fixed formula. What is prescribed is the response of the heart: to receive Jesus gladly and to let that welcome alter our dealings with people we have wronged and people in need.

The parable is a story about a kingdom's founding, not a pattern of how a ruler should behave. The nobleman's severity in verse 27 describes the judgment that awaits those who refuse the King, and it does not authorise anyone to use violence for religious ends. The details of banking and interest do not make the parable a lesson in investment either. Luke records that the master calls the nobleman's money his own and asks what each servant earned, so the lesson is faithful use of what has been entrusted, and the sums are illustrations. In applying the story, we should not read the master's description as harsh as true of God. The servant says it, and the master turns that word against him, verse 22. We are meant to take from the parable the call to serve in the King's absence, the certainty of a reckoning and the shocking generosity with which faithful servants are repaid.

debates.question: Does Zacchaeus announce what he will do, or what he already does?

views.label: A decision made on the spot
views.case: The verbs I give and I will repay are in the present tense in Greek, and many take them as a firm resolve, a present of intention, spoken as he stands before the Lord. This fits the sudden turn of the scene: Jesus has just come to his house, and Zacchaeus responds with a promise. Jesus then says salvation has come, confirming a changed man.

views.label: A defence of his customary practice
views.case: Others hold that the Greek is naturally a habitual present: I give half my possessions to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I repay fourfold. On this view Zacchaeus is answering the crowd's grumbling by pointing to what he regularly does, and Jesus declares him a true son of Abraham despite his reputation. The verse 7 murmuring is then answered with evidence, not with a new resolution.

debates.bearing: On both readings Jesus does not say that salvation has come because of the offer. He says it has come to the house because this man too is a son of Abraham, and the offer is the sign. The grammar is genuinely open, and the doctrine does not hang on it.

debates.question: Is the third servant a picture of an unbeliever or of a false disciple?

views.label: A person who never knew the master
views.case: He says the master is harsh and that he was afraid, verse 21. The master condemns him as wicked and takes away even what he has. On this reading he represents those who refuse the King's rule in their hearts while appearing to belong to the household.

views.label: A believer who fails to serve
views.case: Some argue that because he is called a servant and is among those summoned, he is a believer who loses a reward, not salvation. The judgment, on this view, concerns the usefulness of a life, and the words taken from him refer to opportunity and honour.

debates.bearing: The master's verdict, You wicked servant, and the saying that the one who has not will lose even what he has, are severe. The safe application is that the parable calls every hearer to faithful trust in a master who is not harsh, since the servant's fear was founded on a false picture of him.

debates.question: What does verse 27 say about the fate of the King's enemies?

views.label: A picture of final judgment
views.case: The enemies are those who would not have the King rule over them, and they are slain in his presence. In the context of Luke 19:41 to 44 and 21, some see here also the coming judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70. Others take it as the last judgment at the return of Christ.

views.label: A feature of the story, not a doctrine
views.case: Verse 27 is the nobleman's final act, which fits the Herodian background and the drama of the parable. The point is that refusing the King has consequences, and the verse need not be pressed for detailed teaching on the nature of the judgment.

debates.bearing: All readings agree that the story ends with a decisive reckoning. The tone is a warning to the hearers, in a chapter that moves directly to the King's arrival in Jerusalem, where He is rejected by those who say they do not want Him.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to look at is the one in verse 5, dei, I must stay at your house today. Luke uses this verb of divine necessity, as in 2:49, 4:43 and 24:7, where it marks what must happen because God has willed it. Jesus does not say it would be nice to visit; He says it is necessary. The man who tried to see Jesus finds that Jesus has been seeking him. Verse 5 also gives the word semeron, today, which in Luke carries the sense of salvation now arrived, 2:11, 4:21, 23:43, and appears again in verse 9.

Zacchaeus is described as a chief tax collector, architelones, a title for the head of a customs office, and the word does not occur elsewhere in the New Testament. He is also small in stature. The Greek helikia can mean age or height, and the BSB takes it of height. He climbs a sykomorea, the sycamore fig, a sturdy tree with low branches that suits a short man in a hurry. The detail adds a note of comedy and of humility: a man of dignity climbs a tree in public.

His words in verse 8 use two verbs. I give is didomi, and I will repay is apodidomi, which means to give back what is owed. The first is a gift, the second restitution. The word for cheated is sykophanteo, to accuse falsely or extort, and it is the word John the Baptist used when he told soldiers not to extort, Luke 3:14. The word for fourfold, tetraplous, is the standard of Exodus 22:1 for stolen sheep.

Verse 10 holds the great verbs. The Son of Man came zeteo, to seek, and sozo, to save, and the object is the apolololos, a perfect participle meaning the one who is and remains lost. Luke has used the verb apollymi throughout chapter 15 for the lost sheep, coin and son, 15:4, 6, 8, 24, 32. The seeking is more than an invitation: the verb suggests a search that carries on until it finds. Sozo is the same verb as in 18:26 and 18:42, so the whole sequence from the camel to the blind man to Zacchaeus is a single answer to the question Who then can be saved?

In the parable the key word in verse 13 is pragmateuomai, translated conduct business, a verb of trading. The master's expectation is that the money will be put to work. The third servant keeps his mina in a soudarion, a piece of cloth, the word for a handkerchief or napkin, and the same word is used for the cloth around Lazarus's face, John 11:44, and for the napkin in Jesus' tomb, John 20:7. It is a small, domestic thing, which makes the servant's burial of a king's money look the more careless.

The rewards are given in terms of exousia, authority, over cities in verses 17 and 19. Authority is the very thing the rebellious subjects will not grant the king, verse 14, and the servants are given it in the kingdom. And the master's judgment comes from the servant's own mouth, in verse 22, ek tou stomatos sou, out of your own mouth. The master does not accept the description, he uses it as an argument: if you knew I was demanding, you should have done at least what the banks do. Even on the servant's own picture of him, his behaviour was unreasonable.

typology.fulfillment: In Ezekiel 34:11 to 16 the LORD says He Himself will search for His sheep, rescue them and bring them home, and He faults the shepherds of Israel who had not sought the lost. In Zacchaeus the promise is kept in a person. Jesus calls the man by name, goes to his house and brings him home to the family of Abraham. John says the Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and Paul says that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, 1 Timothy 1:15. The type is more than fulfilled, for the shepherd does not only find the lost but takes their place. It still points beyond itself to the day when all the flock is gathered, Revelation 7:17.

typology.type: The tree and the one who climbs it, Luke 19:4 to 6
typology.fulfillment: A man gets above the crowd and is seen by God, and Scripture often pictures people seeking God from a distance. Here the longing to see Jesus is met by a visit. The story is a small image of grace coming down to meet human reaching. In the end it points to the cross, a tree on which Jesus was lifted up, John 3:14 to 15 and Galatians 3:13. The tree in Jericho is where the sinner is found, and the tree at Jerusalem is where the sinner is saved. This is a suggestive echo more than a type, since Luke does not draw the connection, and it should be held lightly.

typology.type: The nobleman who goes away to receive a kingdom, Luke 19:12
typology.fulfillment: The journey to a distant country and the return as king is a picture of the ascension and the second coming. Daniel 7:13 to 14 describes one like a son of man coming to the Ancient of Days and being given dominion, glory and a kingdom. Jesus goes to the Father to receive that kingdom, Acts 1:9 to 11, and will return, Acts 1:11. Hebrews 10:12 to 13 says that He sat down at the right hand of God and waits until His enemies are made a footstool. The parable falls short in its picture of the king, who is harsh in a way that Christ is not, and who profits from his servants, while Christ gives everything to His.

typology.type: The servants given a trust, Luke 19:13 to 19
typology.fulfillment: God gave Adam the garden to work and keep, Genesis 2:15, and entrusted Israel with the oracles of God, Romans 3:2. In the parable the servants are trusted with the King's money, and in the church the trust is the gospel and the gifts of the Spirit, 2 Timothy 1:14 and 1 Corinthians 12:7. Faithful use brings authority in the coming kingdom, which Paul echoes when he says that believers will judge the world, 1 Corinthians 6:2, and Revelation 3:21 promises that the one who conquers will sit with Christ on His throne. The correspondence falls short in the sums: the servants make their profit with the master's money, and the final reward is vastly greater than the work.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most plainly in verse 10, where Jesus says what He is for: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. That is not a description of a teacher who points the way but of a person who goes to find people. Zacchaeus is not looking for a saviour; he is looking for a view. Jesus is the one who stops under the tree. The story therefore reverses the picture of a religion in which sinners must climb to God. God has come into the street.

The title Son of Man in verse 10 is the same title used of the figure of Daniel 7 who receives a kingdom, and the parable that follows is about that kingdom. Jesus is both: the seeking Son of Man who dines with a tax collector, and the one who goes to a far country to receive kingship and will return. The two scenes are not contradictory. The humble guest of Jericho is the nobleman of the parable, and the power that seeks sinners now is the power that will judge those who refuse Him later.

Notice what the story says about Jesus' authority to declare salvation. He does not wait for a sacrifice or a priest. He says Today salvation has come to this house, with the authority of the One who forgave the paralysed man, 5:20 to 24, and the sinful woman, 7:48. Luke has been building a case that Jesus does what God does. The grumblers in verse 7 object to the company He keeps, but the real offence is that He speaks as the Lord who brings salvation. Zacchaeus himself calls Him Lord, verse 8, as a man who has recognised who has come.

The parable says that the King will go away and return. That is the pattern of the gospel itself: Christ goes up and will come again, Acts 1:11. The faithful servants who are told Well done, good servant are promised the joy of their master, Matthew 25:21, and the authority of the kingdom. What the Lord asks is not that we make Him rich but that we trust Him enough to use what He has given. The third servant did not know the master. Zacchaeus did, and so he could give.

A caution applies to the parable. The nobleman is not simply a portrait of Christ in every detail. His taking of what he did not sow is the servant's accusation, and the master turns it on him; it is not offered as true of Christ, who gives freely and does not withhold. The parable is used to say that the King is coming back, that He will reckon with all who have been trusted with His gifts, and that those who refuse Him will meet a final verdict. The link to Jesus is clear in Luke's own placing of it: the next scene is His royal approach to Jerusalem, where the very rejection the parable foresees begins to take place.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who takes the initiative. Zacchaeus is the one who climbs the tree, yet it is Jesus who stops, looks up and calls him by name. The word dei, I must, speaks of a divine purpose that precedes the man's effort. Salvation here is not found by clever seeking. It is the fruit of a God who has resolved to seek, which is the theology of Ezekiel 34 and of the opening of Genesis 3, where God comes into the garden and asks the hiding man where he is.

It also shows a God who is not put off by reputation. The crowd cannot imagine that the holy man will go to a sinner's house. But the holiness of God in Luke is not a holiness that avoids contamination. It is a holiness that cleanses what it touches, as in the healing of the leper in 5:13. God does not wait for Zacchaeus to be respectable. He is gracious first, and the change of heart follows.

God is also the one who entrusts. The master gives the same sum, a mina, to each of ten servants, which suggests that what is given is the same and the use that is made of it differs. The generosity of the reward, authority over ten cities for the faithful use of a single mina, shows a God who repays far more than service deserves. Jesus says in Luke 12:37 that the master will serve those servants who are watching when he returns. The goodness of God is out of proportion to our effort.

At the same time the passage says God is judge. The nobleman who returns as king is not indulgent. He holds his servants to account, takes from the one who hid his mina, and orders the destruction of the enemies who refused him. The parable will not let us make God's kindness a sentimental thing. A kingdom has a King, and a King has the right to ask who submitted. Paul holds the two together in Romans 11:22, Consider the kindness and severity of God, and Luke has placed them side by side in one chapter.

There is also a tension about God's character. The servant calls the master harsh and uses the charge as an excuse. The master answers by showing that even by that logic the servant was at fault. The parable thus rejects a picture of God as a hard taskmaster who deserves to be feared, and it also shows what such a picture does: it paralyses. Real fear of the Lord, as in Psalm 130:4, is the beginning of obedience, because it stands next to forgiveness.

For worship this means coming to God the way Zacchaeus did, gladly, with a willingness to be found and to let the encounter change what we do with our possessions. It means serving in the King's absence without fear, because we know His character. And it means taking His return seriously, as a day when everything we have been given will be reckoned.

crossReferences.note: The LORD says He will search for His scattered sheep, bring them home and bind up the injured, and He accuses the shepherds of Israel of failing to seek the lost. Luke 19:10 is the fulfilment of that word. The Son of Man takes the role God reserved for Himself, which is why the grumbling crowd is wrong to judge His visit to Zacchaeus.

When someone has wronged a neighbour and confessed it, he must restore what he took in full and add a fifth. Zacchaeus goes far beyond that figure. Reading the law beside his promise shows that his fourfold repayment is an act of generosity beyond obligation, the fruit of the transformation Jesus recognises in verse 9.

The law sets a penalty of five oxen for a stolen ox and four sheep for a stolen sheep, the highest rate of restitution in the Torah. By choosing the fourfold measure Zacchaeus treats every person he may have cheated as a victim of real theft, and he pays the penalty of the law without being compelled to do so.

The Pharisees and scribes grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them, and He answers with the lost sheep and the lost coin. Luke 19:7 repeats the grumbling and verse 10 repeats the answer. Zacchaeus is the living example of the sheep that is found, and the party in heaven over one sinner who repents is realised in his house.

The rich ruler could not part with his wealth and went away sad, and Jesus said how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom. Zacchaeus is the answer to the question of verse 26 about who can be saved. What is impossible with man, a rich man letting go of his possessions, has become possible with God.

Paul says that those who are of faith are sons of Abraham, and that Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith. Jesus calls Zacchaeus a son of Abraham in Luke 19:9 before any such argument has been made, and his joyful welcome of Jesus is the faith that Paul would later describe.

Matthew's parable of the talents shares its skeleton with the minas: a master leaves, servants are entrusted with money, one buries his, and the reckoning rewards the faithful and punishes the fearful. The differences show that Jesus told such stories more than once and shaped them to the setting. In Luke the setting is the expectation of the kingdom at once.

The nations conspire against the LORD and His anointed and say they will not be ruled, and God sets His King on Zion and warns the rulers to serve the LORD with fear. The subjects in Luke 19:14 who say they do not want this man to rule over them are in the same position. The psalm ends with a blessing for those who take refuge in the King.

Whoever is faithful in a very small matter is faithful also in much, and the one who is unrighteous in the little is unrighteous in much. The master's words to the first servant in 19:17 echo this principle precisely. The faithful use of a small thing is the test and the training for a larger trust.

Paul calls himself a servant of Christ and a steward of the mysteries of God, and says that what is required of stewards is that they be found faithful. He leaves the final judgment to the Lord, who will bring to light what is hidden. It is the same expectation as the reckoning of Luke 19:15 to 26, applied to the work of the apostles.

study.oneStory:
The story of Zacchaeus is a small piece of a very large story. In the beginning God made human beings to be generous stewards of His creation, to work the garden and keep it, and to share in His rule. The fall turned stewardship into grasping, and money, like the fruit of Genesis 3, became a thing to seize. The history of Israel is full of the same pattern: a people entrusted with the land and the law, who used them for themselves. The prophets denounced those who added field to field and ground down the poor, Isaiah 5:8, and they promised a day when God would shepherd His people Himself.

When Jesus enters Jericho He steps into that history. Jericho was the first city of the promised land, and Joshua's first act was to see it fall. Zacchaeus, a man who has made his house by taking, is hardly the kind of person the people of that city would have expected the Lord to visit. When Jesus says that salvation has come to the house, grace arrives in the very town where Israel's conquest once began. Rahab was saved from that same city, Joshua 6:25, and now another outsider is found. The family of Abraham is being gathered again.

The parable then widens the lens. A King has been promised since Genesis 49:10 and 2 Samuel 7, and Israel's own kings had been a poor shadow of him. Jesus tells His followers that this king must first go away to receive a kingdom, and that the time before his return is the time of the church. What the servants do in that interval is the story of Acts and of every Christian generation: the gospel is entrusted, and it is put to work. Peter, Paul and the others multiply the gift, and the harvest is the nations.

The parable also anticipates the rejection that will follow in Jerusalem. The subjects who say we do not want this man to rule over us are voiced on the Friday by the crowd who cry that they have no king but Caesar, John 19:15. And yet the pattern of the story is that rejection does not cancel the kingdom: the king returns, and His rule is established.

The end of the story is the new creation, in which the faithful hear well done and share the rule of the King. Revelation 22:5 says that His servants will reign for ever and ever, and Revelation 21:24 pictures the kings of the earth bringing their glory into the city. Wealth, which here divided the ruler from the kingdom and Zacchaeus from his neighbours, is finally redeemed. Everything that was hoarded is given up, and everything that was given for the King's sake is found again. A tax collector who climbed a tree is among those who see the King at last, and the King calls him by name.

quiz.q: What does Jesus declare about Zacchaeus?

options.text: That salvation has come to his house, for the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.
options.note: Luke 19:9-10 announces salvation and states Jesus' seeking, saving mission.

options.text: That Zacchaeus earned his place by giving to the poor.
options.note: The giving is the fruit of salvation already come, not the price that earns it.

options.text: That Zacchaeus is a true son of Abraham, restored by grace.
options.note: True and stated, but it omits the climactic mission statement that the Son of Man seeks and saves the lost.

options.text: That Jesus should not have entered a sinner's house.
options.note: That is the crowd's grumble, which Jesus overturns by declaring salvation.

quiz.q: How does Zacchaeus respond to Jesus?

options.text: He welcomes Jesus joyfully and pledges half his goods to the poor and fourfold repayment to any he cheated.
options.note: Luke 19:6-8 shows joyful welcome and concrete, generous repentance.

options.text: He promises to give generously to the poor.
options.note: True, but it omits the fourfold restitution and the joyful welcome that mark his repentance.

options.text: He feels guilty but keeps his wealth.
options.note: The opposite; he gladly parts with his wealth in genuine repentance.

options.text: He hides from Jesus in shame.
options.note: He climbed a tree to see Jesus and welcomed Him joyfully.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus tell the parable of the ten minas?

options.text: Because the crowd thought the kingdom would appear immediately, so He teaches that the King must go and return.
options.note: Luke 19:11 gives the reason: to correct expectations of an instant kingdom.

options.text: To teach that the kingdom's arrival was delayed.
options.note: True in effect, but it misses that He specifically addresses their expectation of an immediate kingdom.

options.text: To warn against investing money carelessly.
options.note: The minas illustrate stewardship of what the King entrusts, not financial advice.

options.text: To announce that the kingdom had already fully come.
options.note: The parable corrects that very idea; the King departs before returning to reign.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the faithful servants from the third servant?

options.text: The faithful put the mina to work and are rewarded, while the third hid it in fear and is condemned.
options.note: Luke 19:16-24 rewards faithful labor and judges fearful inaction.

options.text: The faithful earned more money than the third servant.
options.note: True on the surface, but the deeper issue is faithful stewardship versus fearful, fruitless hiding.

options.text: The third servant lost the mina entirely.
options.note: He kept it safe in a cloth; his fault was fearful inaction, not losing it.

options.text: The master rewarded all the servants equally.
options.note: Rewards matched faithfulness, and the fearful servant lost even his mina.

quiz.q: What does the fate of the rebellious citizens picture?

options.text: The judgment awaiting those who refuse the reign of the returning King.
options.note: Luke 19:14,27 portrays, in an ancient king's terms, the judgment on those who reject his rule.

options.text: That rejecting the King brings serious consequences.
options.note: True but soft; the parable pictures decisive judgment, not merely consequences.

options.text: A call for Jesus' followers to punish His enemies.
options.note: It is a parabolic image of divine judgment, not a mandate for human vengeance.

options.text: That the King is powerless against those who oppose Him.
options.note: The opposite: the King returns with full authority to judge.

questions: Zacchaeus only wanted to see Jesus, but Jesus was seeking him. Where in your story can you see that God was searching for you before you ever reached for Him?
Salvation showed itself in Zacchaeus's open hands and honest restitution. If grace has truly reached you, where should it be reshaping how you handle money and past wrongs?
The crowd wanted the kingdom to appear instantly. Where are you impatient for God to act now, and how does the promise of the returning King steady you in the meantime?
The faithful servants put a little to work; the fearful one buried it. What has the King entrusted to you, and are you investing it or hiding it out of fear?
The citizens said, we do not want this man to rule over us. Is there any area of your life where you are quietly refusing the reign of the King?

translationNotes.note: A mina was a sum of money, likely a silver coin worth about a hundred days' wages; each servant received one. The equal starting amount, unlike the varied talents of Matthew 25, sharpens the focus on faithfulness with the same trust.

The picture of a nobleman traveling to a distant country to receive kingship recalls Archelaus, who went to Rome for his crown while a delegation of his subjects opposed him. Jesus uses the familiar scene to speak of His own departure and return.

'A son of Abraham' declares Zacchaeus a true heir of the promise, not by his descent, which he already had, but by the faith and repentance that grace produced, a theme the New Testament develops for all who believe.
